title: Bread on the waters
hook: cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
tomorrow: the Preacher's last poem: a house falling quiet. whose house?

segments.voice: Six days, two books. Yan Hui's temper: learn and practice. Zilu's two halves: that is knowledge. The mirror: examine myself. Confucius's life: my decades. The Preacher's breath, vapour. And yesterday's sun and rivers: nothing new. Now, one more piece of the Preacher's advice.
screen: `LEARN AND PRACTICE · THAT IS KNOWLEDGE · EXAMINE MYSELF` → `MY DECADES · BREATH, VAPOUR · NOTHING NEW`

segments.voice: You hold a door, push a stranger's stalled car to the curb, leave a big tip in a town you're only driving through. You'll never know how any of those stories ends. Near the close of Ecclesiastes, after all the breath and the circling sun, the Preacher gives a strange piece of advice: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days."
screen: `STORIES YOU NEVER SEE END.` → `CAST THY BREAD UPON THE WATERS.`

segments.voice: Bread on a river looks like waste. Readers have heard it two ways. Some hear trade: send your grain out on ships, and in time it comes back. Others, Jewish and Christian readers alike, hear generosity: give where you can't see the return. Either way, the next lines lean on not knowing. "Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth." Whoever keeps watching the wind, Qoheleth says, never sows. "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that." Here's the teaching, and it's a turn in this book. Hevel, life's brevity and our not knowing, isn't a reason to hold back. It's the reason to scatter. You can't control which good thing lands, so do more than one, morning and evening. One to tell a friend tonight: in Ecclesiastes, uncertainty is an argument for generosity, not against it.
screen: `TRADE, OR GENEROSITY?` · `A PORTION TO SEVEN, AND TO EIGHT.` · `WHOEVER WATCHES THE WIND WON'T SOW.` · `NOT KNOWING IS THE REASON TO GIVE.` · then, large: `BREAD ON THE WATERS.`

segments.voice: Do one small giving now, where you'll never see the result: put a coin or a note aside for the next tip jar, leave a kind unsigned note for a neighbor, set a book by the door to leave where someone will find it. Let it go like bread on moving water. Don't follow it with your eyes; let the current have it.
Bread on the waters: give it to the current, because you don't know which seed will grow.
Your line: bread on the waters. Not knowing is a reason to give, not to wait. That's the week.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 11:1 is quoted in Jewish and Christian settings as a call to generosity; some readers take it as advice about sea trade. Either way the passage stresses acting without knowing the outcome.
